title: Closing One Eye to Map a Critical Period
endLine: Control sensory input across ages to reveal when experience wires circuits.

scenes.tts: How do you test when experience wires a developing brain? Close one eye briefly, then listen to cortex. Sensory deprivation alters input at a chosen age to watch circuits rewire.
scenes.caption: How do you test when experience wires a developing brain? Close one eye briefly, then listen to cortex. Sensory deprivation alters input at a chosen age to watch circuits rewire.
scenes.visual: Schematic cross-section filling over 60% of frame height: two open eyes send bright rhythmic pulse streams into a sheet of visual cortex; the opening question appears cleanly above; then one eyelid gently closes, its pulse stream dims, and a recording probe settles onto one cortical neuron. High contrast, at most 6 elements, labels 5 words or fewer.
scenes.narration: How do you test when experience wires a developing brain? Close one eye briefly, then listen to cortex. Sensory deprivation alters input at a chosen age to watch circuits rewire.

scenes.visual: Hold the schematic eyes-to-cortex world with gentle ambient pulse motion while the film title 'Closing One Eye to Map a Critical Period' appears cleanly for 1.8 seconds and fades out.

scenes.tts: Start in primary visual cortex, the first cortical stop for signals from the eyes. In its binocular zone, most neurons answer both eyes. Contralateral means opposite side; ipsilateral means same side. Most mouse cells answer the contralateral eye more strongly.
scenes.caption: Start in primary visual cortex, the first cortical stop for signals from the eyes. In its binocular zone, most neurons answer both eyes. Contralateral means opposite side; ipsilateral means same side. Most mouse cells answer the contralateral eye more strongly.
scenes.visual: Same schematic eyes-to-cortex world carried in place. The binocular zone highlights around the recorded neuron before narration names it. Labels 'Contralateral' (opposite side, strong bright pulse stream) and 'Ipsilateral' (same side, dimmer pulse stream) appear as each eye is named; ambient pulses keep moving.
scenes.narration: Start in primary visual cortex, the first cortical stop for signals from the eyes. In its binocular zone, most neurons answer both eyes. Contralateral means opposite side; ipsilateral means same side. Most mouse cells answer the contralateral eye more strongly.

scenes.tts: Score preference with the ocular dominance index: contralateral minus ipsilateral, divided by their sum. An illustrative cell fires thirty spikes a second to contralateral input, ten to ipsilateral. Thirty minus ten is twenty; thirty plus ten is forty. Twenty over forty is zero point five zero. Plus one is contralateral only; minus one, ipsilateral only.
scenes.caption: Score preference with the ocular dominance index: contralateral minus ipsilateral, divided by their sum. An illustrative cell fires 30 spikes a second to contralateral input, 10 to ipsilateral. 30 − 10 is 20; 30 + 10 is 40. 20 ÷ 40 is 0.50. +1 is contralateral only; −1, ipsilateral only.
scenes.visual: Same schematic eyes-to-cortex diagram shifts slightly left to reveal a large horizontal gauge from −1 (Ipsilateral) to +1 (Contralateral) and the formula (C − I) / (C + I), tagged 'illustrative example'. As 30 and 10 are spoken, spike bars rise to 30 and 10 (computed from the illustrative numbers), substitute into (30 − 10) / (30 + 10) = 20 / 40 = 0.50, and the gauge needle glides smoothly to +0.50.
scenes.narration: Score preference with the ocular dominance index: contralateral minus ipsilateral, divided by their sum. An illustrative cell fires 30 spikes a second to contralateral input, 10 to ipsilateral. 30 − 10 is 20; 30 + 10 is 40. 20 ÷ 40 is 0.50. +1 is contralateral only; −1, ipsilateral only.

scenes.tts: Now suture the contralateral eyelid shut, letting only diffuse light enter. This is monocular deprivation. At postnatal day twenty-eight, about four days of closure weaken that eye's responses. The index drops and can fall below zero, favoring the open eye. Change input at one age, and measure what rewires.
scenes.caption: Now suture the contralateral eyelid shut, letting only diffuse light enter. This is monocular deprivation. At postnatal day 28, about four days of closure weaken that eye's responses. The index drops and can fall below zero, favoring the open eye. Change input at one age, and measure what rewires.
scenes.visual: Same eyes-to-cortex world and −1 to +1 gauge, with a schematic age timeline scrubber added along the bottom at P28. The contralateral eyelid closes with a neat lid suture and its stream softens to dim diffuse light; the label 'Monocular deprivation' appears as it is named. As the scrubber advances about 4 days, the contralateral spike bar shrinks (schematic) and the gauge needle slides from +0.50 past 0 into negative territory toward the open ipsilateral eye (schematic: 'can fall below zero').
scenes.narration: Now suture the contralateral eyelid shut, letting only diffuse light enter. This is monocular deprivation. At postnatal day 28, about four days of closure weaken that eye's responses. The index drops and can fall below zero, favoring the open eye. Change input at one age, and measure what rewires.

scenes.tts: Yet closing one eye fits two ideas: simple disuse, or competition between eyes. In an illustrative model, give an open eye ten units of useful activity and a sutured eye one. If you close both eyes instead, what does each idea predict?
scenes.caption: Yet closing one eye fits two ideas: simple disuse, or competition between eyes. In an illustrative model, give an open eye 10 units of useful activity and a sutured eye 1. If you close both eyes instead, what does each idea predict?
scenes.visual: Same eyes-to-cortex schematic, tagged 'illustrative model, not measured'. First the open eye pulses with a '10' badge and the sutured eye with a '1' badge. Then the second eyelid closes too so both eyes show '1'. Below, two empty slots labeled 'Disuse: ?' and 'Competition: ?' settle cleanly on screen.
scenes.narration: Yet closing one eye fits two ideas: simple disuse, or competition between eyes. In an illustrative model, give an open eye 10 units of useful activity and a sutured eye 1. If you close both eyes instead, what does each idea predict?

scenes.visual: Deliberate 4.5-second thinking pause. Hold the both-eyes-shut schematic (1 vs 1) with the question 'Both eyes shut: Disuse vs. Competition?' and the two empty slots while a quiet 4.5-second progress bar fills smoothly along the bottom.

scenes.tts: Under disuse, a sutured eye keeps one of ten units, ten percent, either way. Under competition, its share is its activity divided by the sum. With one eye closed, one divided by eleven is about nine percent. With both closed, one divided by two stays fifty percent, separating the ideas.
scenes.caption: Under disuse, a sutured eye keeps 1 of 10 units, 10%, either way. Under competition, its share is its activity divided by the sum. With one eye closed, 1 ÷ 11 is about 9%. With both closed, 1 ÷ 2 stays 50%, separating the ideas.
scenes.visual: Same both-eyes-shut schematic. The 'Disuse' slot fills first with '1 / 10 = 10%' for both one-eye-closed and both-eyes-closed. Next the 'Competition' slot reveals formula 'B ÷ (A + B)' (computed from the illustrative model): for one eye closed, '1 ÷ 11 ≈ 9%' appears; for both closed, '1 ÷ 2 = 50%' pops bright beside 10%, separating the two predictions.
scenes.narration: Under disuse, a sutured eye keeps 1 of 10 units, 10%, either way. Under competition, its share is its activity divided by the sum. With one eye closed, 1 ÷ 11 is about 9%. With both closed, 1 ÷ 2 stays 50%, separating the ideas.

scenes.tts: Another check locates the change. The closed eye's retina and L G N, its relay to cortex, still respond. Test adults too, and sample the whole age curve, not one number. In this film's terms, a critical period shuts abruptly like a door. A sensitive period fades gradually, like a tide going out.
scenes.caption: Another check locates the change. The closed eye's retina and LGN, its relay to cortex, still respond. Test adults too, and sample the whole age curve, not one number. In this film's terms, a critical period shuts abruptly like a door. A sensitive period fades gradually, like a tide going out.
scenes.visual: Same eyes-to-cortex schematic: active pulse indicators light up at the retina and at the LGN (labelled 'LGN: relay to cortex') along the closed eye's pathway to show they still respond. Along the bottom age timeline, two schematic outcome curves draw in: a sharp step-down curve labeled 'Critical period' (door shutting) and a gentle sloped decline labeled 'Sensitive period' (tide going out), tagged 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Another check locates the change. The closed eye's retina and LGN, its relay to cortex, still respond. Test adults too, and sample the whole age curve, not one number. scenes.tts: In nineteen sixty-three, Wiesel and Hubel closed one kitten eye near birth for about three months. Very few cortical cells answered the closed eye, yet its retina and L G N still responded. An adult cat showed no change. In infant macaques, Hubel, Wiesel and Simon LeVay traced each eye's stripes of territory in layer four C. Open-eye stripes widened; closed-eye stripes narrowed.
scenes.caption: In 1963, Wiesel and Hubel closed one kitten eye near birth for about three months. Very few cortical cells answered the closed eye, yet its retina and LGN still responded. An adult cat showed no change. In infant macaques, Hubel, Wiesel and Simon LeVay traced each eye's stripes of territory in layer 4C. Open-eye stripes widened; closed-eye stripes narrowed.
scenes.visual: Same eyes-to-cortex world transforms to show two clean findings in sequence (schematic): first, a kitten cortex with nearly silent closed-eye input while retina and LGN pulse strongly, paired with an unchanged adult cat gauge (tag: 'Wiesel & Hubel, 1963'); second, alternating stripes of each eye's territory in layer 4C morph so open-eye stripes widen and closed-eye stripes narrow (tag: 'Hubel, Wiesel & LeVay').
scenes.narration: In 1963, Wiesel and Hubel closed one kitten eye near birth for about three months. Very few cortical cells answered the closed eye, yet its retina and LGN still responded. An adult cat showed no change. In infant macaques, Hubel, Wiesel and Simon LeVay traced each eye's stripes of territory in layer 4C. Open-eye stripes widened; closed-eye stripes narrowed.

scenes.tts: In nineteen ninety-six, Gordon and Stryker varied the age of monocular deprivation in mice. The shift was largest around day twenty-eight, much smaller before about day nineteen or after about day thirty-two. Those ages hold for mouse visual cortex, not for song or language. Changing input across ages, with controls, reveals when experience wires circuits.
scenes.caption: In 1996, Gordon and Stryker varied the age of monocular deprivation in mice. The shift was largest around day 28, much smaller before about day 19 or after about day 32. Those ages hold for mouse visual cortex, not for song or language. Changing input across ages, with controls, reveals when experience wires circuits.
scenes.visual: Same age timeline scrubber sweeps from P19 through P28 to P32 above a schematic mouse shift curve that peaks around P28 and sits low before about P19 and after about P32 (tag: 'Gordon & Stryker, 1996; schematic'). A brief scope note 'Mouse visual cortex only' appears as the full eyes-to-cortex world settles cleanly.
scenes.narration: In 1996, Gordon and Stryker varied the age of monocular deprivation in mice. The shift was largest around day 28, much smaller before about day 19 or after about day 32. Those ages hold for mouse visual cortex, not for song or language. Changing input across ages, with controls, reveals when experience wires circuits.
